What Keynes found when he opened Newton’s trunks
A flawed, complex man, and the accidents that raised him

brief.head: All fit, no theory
brief.text: Kepler’s laws fit Tycho Brahe’s data beautifully, Ajay Shah said, but like an AI model they could not say why. Newton derived them from first principles. {007-C01}

brief.head: Ivory tower, no thanks
brief.text: Researchers who only look at each other are fundamentally sterile, Ajay Shah said. Ideas and markets are one continuum: firms bring hard problems, thinkers fuel business. {007-C04}

brief.head: Defeats that mobilised
brief.text: Almost every satyagraha Gandhi led failed in its immediate aims, Amit Varma said. Yet each mobilised ordinary people, which no leader before him had managed. {007-C06}

brief.head: More dots, please
brief.text: Gandhi, Ram Guha writes, said he did not need to read because he could see the world unfold. Amit Varma called it a rationalisation: reading gives more dots to connect. {007-C13}

brief.head: Wrong, and wonderful
brief.text: Ajay Shah disagrees with John Maynard Keynes on almost all his economics, and counts him among the most wonderful people who ever lived. Amit Varma said ditto. {007-C12}

thought.text: We should not be reverential, we should be analytical, we should understand.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, urging an analytical rather than devotional reading of Gandhi and his ideas

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on Newton, Gandhi and history
lead.head: The alchemist and the accident
body: Is genius made by its times, or does it arrive by accident? Ajay Shah answered with Isaac Newton, Amit Varma with Mohandas Gandhi, and they did not quite agree.

Shah told Newton’s story in three chapters. The first is the one children hear: plague shut down Cambridge, Newton went to live with his grandmother, and in one feverish year he built everything. {007-S02}

The second came from John Maynard Keynes, who bought many of Newton’s papers and found them full of alchemy and the Bible. “He says Newton was not the first man of the age of reason, he was the last of the magicians,” Shah said. {007-C02}
The third came from Boris Hessen, a Soviet physicist and philosopher who asked, in 1931, what kind of society produces a Newton.
## England’s conditions
Hessen’s answer, as Shah relayed it, was 17th-century England: Protestant enough for free thought, a seafaring power learning optics and navigation, and protected by the Magna Carta tradition.
“So Newton doesn’t come out of thin air,” Shah said. Gene expression was his metaphor: a society that protects its mavericks lets its Newtons flourish. {007-C03}

Varma accepted the point, up to a point. Newton could not have been Newton in Spain, he said, but the times did not make him inevitable. That such a person was there at that time was “a marvellous accident of history”.
## Gandhi, the outlier

Gandhi, Varma argued, was the counterexample: a black swan. His influences, Tolstoy, Ruskin and a dogmatic vegetarian society in London, were haphazard next to those of the Congress moderates, who read Mill, Bentham and Adam Smith.

His rise was an accident too. Gandhi allied with the Khilafat movement to restore the caliphate in Turkey, while asking for India’s independence. Varma called it utterly incoherent, yet it made Gandhi the leader of the Congress in 1920.

Shah disagreed. Gandhi drew on the best of Hindu and Jain philosophy, he said, and faced the great question of his age: how to reconcile India with the West. “You should think that there were a large number of lotteries and one person got expressed,” he said. {007-C05}

Nonviolence also suited the opponent, Shah argued: under French, Belgian or Japanese rule, a freedom fighter would soon have been jailed and killed. “It required British decency for these kinds of ideas to survive and flourish.”
## Freedom was coming anyway
On one thing the hosts agreed: the story we grow up on, in which the Congress fought the British and India won its freedom, is too simple.

Varma pointed to a Britain broke after the Second World War. Shah added the end of the first globalisation in 1913, Europe’s wars, and the Atlantic Charter, which tied American help to a post-colonial future.
“My counterfactual in history is there is no scenario under which British rule would have lasted in a significant way beyond 1950, 1955,” Shah said. {007-C09}
Hindsight, Varma warned, makes the uncertain look inevitable. “Before it happened, it was probabilistic. Everything is probabilistic, it’s up in the air. After it’s happened, it’s 100% happened.”

The discussion closed on luck. Varma read from his column *Luck is All Around* on the odds against anyone existing; Shah told listeners they were unique strings in DNA’s four-letter alphabet, and should wake up and do amazing things.
Newton, Shah noted, had been shipped off in a lockdown. “What do you have to show for your lockdown achievements?”

second.label: The road to Partition
second.head: The gentleman walks out
second.deck: Amit Varma on how Gandhi’s rise broke the last great moderate
body: With Gokhale and Pherozeshah Mehta gone, Mohammed Ali Jinnah was the last great moderate in the Congress, Amit Varma said: deeply educated, rational, and expected to lead the party. Ram Guha tells how Jinnah once considered going to South Africa, where he and Gandhi might have become business partners. {#partners}

Gandhi’s takeover in 1920 broke him. Jinnah said he was parting company with the Congress and Gandhi, because he did not believe in working up mass hysteria. His sense of self badly hurt, he moved towards the two-nation theory. {007-S11}
Varma traced Partition, and fissures India still wrestles with, back to that moment. A rational man of deep learning, he said, became a completely different person.

quote.text: I do not believe in working up mass hysteria. Politics is a gentleman’s game.

second.caption: Jinnah’s parting of ways

third.head: The outlaw at the Mint
body: Isaac Newton spent his life on alchemy, and it was against the law. In 1404, Ajay Shah said, the British government had banned all forms of alchemy to protect its monopoly on coinage. {#alchemyban}

Nobody then knew that base metals cannot be turned into gold, and the state could not take the risk. Debase the currency, Shah said, and the whole monetary system breaks down. He was, he admitted, stealing words from nervous policymakers of today.
“Newton was this lawbreaker and in case that irony is not adequate, late in his life, Newton became the master of the mint,” Shah said: the governor of the central bank, in today’s terms. {007-S04}
Amit Varma’s verdict: putting an alchemist in charge of the mint “would be like a poacher becoming a gamekeeper”. {007-J06}
third.caption: the alchemist at the Mint

p2.title: Genius or chance?
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s three chapters on Isaac Newton, and Amit Varma’s case that Gandhi was a black swan

sections.label: Newton, part one
sections.head: First the data, then the why
sections.caption: Newton’s lone-genius legend
body: Ajay Shah’s first window on Isaac Newton is the one children learn. Plague shut Cambridge, Newton went to a village to live with his grandmother, and in one feverish year he “just created an immense explosion in the world of knowledge”.

Shah set out the sequence. The old Greek records of the planets were poor and the models muddled: the sun circled the earth, and orbits had to be pure circles, patched with epicycles, “wheels within wheels”. {007-J08}

Copernicus put the sun at the centre but still thought in circles, so his model was only a little better. Then Tycho Brahe built the world’s best data set, and Johannes Kepler found three simple laws that fit it without explaining why. {007-C01}
## First principles
Newton supplied the why. His laws of motion, his law of gravity and his calculus made a first-principles toolkit from which Kepler’s laws dropped out as a consequence. “What a triumph,” Shah said.
Alexander Pope caught the myth in an epitaph: “Nature and her mysteries lay hidden in the night. God said, Let Newton be and all was light.” {007-J09}
How did it happen? Shah could point only to concentration, which Newton shared with Einstein. Beyond that, he said, “we have no great insight”.
~ The party line, he said, is that a genius just happened and should get all the credit. Shah’s second and third chapters made the story “way more interesting”.

quote.text: But statistical models, okay? They’re like an AI that it kind of fits the data, but you don’t know anything about why it works.

sections.label: Newton, part two
sections.head: Reason in public, gold at home
sections.caption: Keynes and the last of the magicians
body: Many years after Newton, Ajay Shah said, someone auctioned off his papers, inherited from a great-grandfather. John Maynard Keynes turned up and put down 9,000 pounds of his own money for a good chunk of them. {#auction}
The rest, Keynes sniffed, had “doubtless ended up in America”, which Shah rendered as America being “the backwaters where things go to die”. {007-J05}

Keynes was the first to study them, and he was aghast. Newton had spent his life on alchemy and the Bible, counting letters in scripture for the secret of making gold. He wrote a million words on alchemy.
## Two Newtons
Keynes’s verdict was that Newton was the last of the magicians, the place where magic and superstition give way to reason. {007-C02}

In public Newton was clean and rational. Asked how gravity worked, he said “I do not make hypotheses”, which Shah translated as “I do not speculate”. {007-J10} Inside, Shah said, he was a tormented man.

The paper, *Newton, the Man*, was meant for 1942, the 300th anniversary of Newton’s birth. The war pushed the conference to 1946, in Warsaw, Shah said; Keynes had died, and his brother Geoffrey presented it.
~ Shah saw a lesson for everyone. Old and new ideas fight inside all of us, he said, as in Nehru’s line about being a battlefield of ideas.

quote.text: He opened those trunks of material and was just aghast at what was going on. Newton was filled with alchemy and the Bible.

sections.label: Newton, part three
sections.head: The making of a Newton
sections.caption: Boris Hessen’s Marxist Newton
body: In 1931 Boris Hessen, a Soviet physicist and philosopher, applied the Marxist approach to history to Newton. {007-R07} That was still a time, Ajay Shah noted, when Marxists held real intellectual leadership.

Hessen asked what social and economic conditions produce a Newton. Shah’s summary of the answer began with freedom. In Italy Giordano Bruno was burnt at the stake and Galileo threatened with torture; Protestant England was freer. “A pretty basic thing is you should not be burning mavericks,” Shah said. {#mavericks}

England had also been the greatest seafaring nation since it destroyed the Spanish Armada in 1588, which meant optics, telescopes, navigation and machines. And under the Magna Carta, Newton could break the alchemy law at home without fear of a dungeon. {007-C03}
## Money and ideas

Hessen’s boldest point, Shah said, was rejecting the “Brahminical” view that ideas stand apart from the base project of making money. Thinkers fuel business, and business brings thinkers its problems. {007-C04}
Amit Varma added that thinkers can be builders: Jeff Bezos, Steve Jobs, Elon Musk and Paul Graham, whose essays he called “just a treasure given to mankind”.
~ Hessen himself was an outspoken free thinker. In 1936, Shah said, he was murdered in one of Stalin’s purges. {007-S05}

quote.text: The wellsprings of the intellectual process emerge from demands made of the thinking people.

sections.label: Gandhi, the case
sections.head: A swan nobody saw coming
sections.caption: Gandhi as a black swan
body: Amit Varma offered Mohandas Gandhi as the counterexample to Ajay Shah’s Newton: not a product of historical currents but a black swan.

VS Naipaul, Varma noted, called Gandhi the least Indian of the Indian leaders. {007-J15} His influences were haphazard: Tolstoy, Ruskin and a London vegetarian society as dogmatic as some vegans today. The Congress moderates, by contrast, read Mill, Bentham and Adam Smith.
## Railways, lawyers, doctors

Varma read from *Hind Swaraj*, written in Gandhi’s early forties, which rails against railways, lawyers and doctors: “Hospitals are institutions for propagating sin.” Gandhi himself later accepted treatment from European doctors.
When Varma asked Ramachandra Guha how a man so wrong could be right about nonviolent resistance, Guha said he was right about the one thing he had personal experience of. {007-S08}
Gandhi’s rise, too, was an accident, Varma argued. His alliance with the Khilafat movement made no sense, yet in 1920 it carried him from the margins to the head of the Congress. {007-S10}

~ Varma thinks of him as “Mohandas Gandhi, not Mahatma Gandhi”, a complex, tortured man. Gandhi’s hundred volumes of writing are free online, and he would have been a blogger today, Varma said. {#blogger}

quote.text: But it turns out, and I believe it turns out by accident, to be a strategic master stroke.

sections.label: Gandhi, the reply
sections.head: One ticket in many lotteries
sections.caption: Gandhi and the ripe conditions
body: Ajay Shah would not let Gandhi be a black swan. His moral philosophy, Shah said, came from the high philosophy of Hinduism and Jainism, on which Tagore and the New Testament were sprinkled.

Gandhi also faced the great question of his age, how to fit India and the West together, as any child today grows up with the regulation of AI. The conditions were ripe, Shah said, for someone to be expressed. {007-C05}
Nonviolence fitted the opponent, too. Britain was ruled by liberal democracy and the rule of law, so an appeal to its decency worked better than Subhas Chandra Bose’s call to pick up guns. {007-C10}
## Tactician or system-builder?
Shah divided men of action into tacticians, who tack with the wind, and system-builders, who seek coherence and so can admit being wrong. Gandhi, he said, was a do-it-yourself philosopher. {007-C08}

Varma disagreed. Gandhi was a tactician, he argued, with a small set of tactics applied rigidly; *Hind Swaraj* is too incoherent to be philosophy. Still, he said, both would agree that everyone should read Gandhi’s writings and study his life.

~ Shah also credited Europe’s self-destruction with easing India’s path. “If Wagner and Russian forces are going to fight it out with each other, it’s easier for Ukraine to go free,” he said. {007-J20}

quote.text: If you are only a tactical man of action, nothing is wrong. Everything is expedient.

side.boxText: *Newton, the Man*, John Maynard Keynes’s paper, is the source of the “last of the magicians” view. Ajay Shah, who disagrees with nearly all of Keynes’s economics, recommends his *Essays in Persuasion* and *Essays in Biography*: “Everybody should dream of writing like that.” {007-R05}

contQuote.text: It tells you how character is contingent, how everything you claim to believe in may be contingent, how we are driven by incentives we cannot understand.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A gift of data, a donkey’s god, a mentor’s order and a wartime bargain

stories.start: there were old Greek databases about the movements of the planets and the stars

stories.caption: Tycho Brahe’s gift to Kepler
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the data behind Newton’s triumph
stories.head: A gift for the man he detested
body: Long before Isaac Newton, astronomy ran on old Greek records of the planets and stars, and the data were poor. The models were worse, Ajay Shah said: the sun went round the earth, and every orbit had to be a pure circle.
When the circles did not fit the data, astronomers added epicycles, wheels within wheels. It was complicated, Shah said, and it was a mess.

Copernicus had the simple idea that the earth goes round the sun. But he still thought in circles, so his model fit only a little better. People mock those who opposed him, Shah said, but as science the gains were not great.

The breakthrough came from a Danish lord, Tycho Brahe, living off the coast on the island of Uraniborg. “You can’t make these things up,” Shah said. Tycho gave his whole life to making the world’s best data set on the movements of the planets and stars.
As his life came to an end, he knew that only one man could make sense of it: Johannes Kepler, whom he truly detested. Without Kepler, his life’s work would be pointless. {007-S01}
“So at the end of his life he swallowed his pride and he handed this data on a platter to Kepler,” Shah said.
~ Kepler found three beautiful, simple laws. The planets move in ellipses. They sweep out equal areas in equal times. And the square of the time is proportional to the cube of the radius.
stories.why: Breakthroughs rest on patient, unglamorous data work, and here on a man who put his life’s work above his pride. Kepler’s laws fit the data without saying why; it took Newton’s first principles to explain them. {007-C01}

stories.start: Gopal Ganesh Shagarkar, who sadly died uh too young, he was a moderate
stories.end: And it it could possibly not be that place today
stories.caption: Agarkar’s question
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on his old college’s irreverent past
stories.head: The professor’s donkey god
body: In the 1890s the reformer Gopal Ganesh Agarkar, a moderate leader who died too young, was teaching a biology class at Fergusson College in Pune.
At one point he asked: “If donkeys had a god, what would that god look like?” After a few moments of silence, Amit Varma said, Agarkar answered with a gesture. {007-S07}
This was in the late 1800s, before the 20th century had even begun, and the college was called, Varma said, “the hotbed of atheism”.
~ Varma studied at Fergusson a century later. “It almost breaks my heart that when I was in Fergusson College, I did not know any of this,” he said. He doubts it could be that place today.
stories.why: Intellectual daring is not a ratchet that only turns one way. A college in late-19th-century Pune allowed an irreverence in its classrooms that, Amit Varma suspects, might be impossible there now.
stories.postscript: Fergusson was also where Gandhi first met his hero, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, on a walk around the grounds.

stories.end: what his reasoning was, but He was a little wacko in some ways.
stories.caption: Gokhale’s last instruction
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a mentor’s last request to Gandhi
stories.head: Look before you lead
body: Gandhi first met his hero, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, in the early 1890s on a walk around the grounds of Fergusson College. When he came back from South Africa for good, the moderates were dying out and Gokhale was ill.
Gokhale had read *Hind Swaraj* and was alarmed, Amit Varma said, because the ideas were nonsense. He saw in Gandhi a man of great conviction and energy who did not yet know the country.
So he asked for a promise. “For the next one year you will not take part in any political activity. You will go around the country and you will just see things.” {007-S09}
~ A month later Gokhale died. Gandhi kept the promise, and as a tribute to Gokhale, for reasons Varma does not know, he did it barefoot. {#barefoot}

quote.text: He was a little wacko in some ways.

stories.start: When uh The second world war started in 1939. Roosevelt was very clear
stories.end: that they were going to have to create some new arrangement in India.
stories.caption: the Atlantic Charter
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on America’s hand in Indian independence
stories.head: Roosevelt’s price for a rescue
body: When the Second World War began in 1939, Ajay Shah said, Roosevelt was clear that America had to be in it on Britain’s side. But a powerful isolationism held him back.

It had three strands. Some racist nationalists would happily have done business with Hitler. Many Americans were exhausted by the First World War and the flu that followed it. And a mistrust of empire dated back to the American revolt of 1776.

Helping Britain could look like supporting the British Empire, which Churchill was determined to protect. Between September 1939 and December 1941 the two leaders argued it out, and the result was the Atlantic Charter.
“Roosevelt basically said to the British that we will come to your aid. But we have to plan for a post-colonial future,” Shah said. {007-S12}
~ Lend-Lease came with conditions about India, Shah said.
stories.why: Indian independence, in Ajay Shah’s telling, was shaped in Washington and London as well as by the freedom movement. The history is well established, he said, but not taught adequately in India, and these are stories worth telling.

quiz.q: Who handed the world’s best planetary data to Johannes Kepler, a man he detested?
quiz.a: Tycho Brahe, the Danish lord, who swallowed his pride at the end of his life.

quiz.q: After reading Newton’s papers, what did Keynes call him instead of the first man of reason?
quiz.a: The last of the magicians, a man torn between alchemy and reason.

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, was Newton’s alchemy research against the law?
quiz.a: In 1404 the British government had banned alchemy, fearing debasement of the currency.

quiz.q: What question did Gopal Ganesh Agarkar put to his biology class at Fergusson College?
quiz.a: If donkeys had a god, what would that god look like?

quiz.q: What promise did the ailing Gokhale extract from Gandhi on his return to India?
quiz.a: A year out of politics, travelling the country to observe; Gandhi did it barefoot.

quiz.q: Asked by a journalist about Western civilisation, what did Gandhi reply, as Shah told it?
quiz.a: That it would be a good idea, a sign of Britain’s lost respect.
